Chapter 11: Guardrails for Intuition—Building Systems That Protect Against Error
Even the sharpest intuition can take a wrong turn now and then. Our minds are quick, capable of split-second judgment, but that speed means we’re always at risk—bias, stress, or just plain inexperience can trip us up.
That’s why the smartest organizations—and the people inside them—don’t just trust their gut. They build systems, little safety nets, that help intuition stay on course.
Picture yourself in an airline cockpit. Pilots are trained to make lightning-fast calls, but they don’t rely on instinct alone. They use strict checklists and well-tested protocols. These aren’t handcuffs—they’re lifelines.
When something’s off, the system is there to catch it before it spirals into a real problem.
And this isn’t just about flying airplanes. Think about hospitals. Surgeons and nurses use checklists, too—even when they’re racing against the clock. These routines don’t take away from their skill. If anything, they make those quick judgments even more trustworthy, because there’s a safety net to catch the little things that might otherwise slip by.
There’s a great example from a hospital that brought in a simple checklist for central line insertions—a routine but risky procedure. What happened? Infections dropped dramatically. The doctors didn’t get less skilled; their intuition just got a boost, because the checklist caught small mistakes in a hectic environment.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? Intuition is at its best when it’s supported by systems designed to minimize errors. It’s not about ignoring that gut feeling—it’s about creating habits, routines, and guardrails that keep those instincts true.
Blind auditions in music, standardized interviews during hiring, clear protocols in high-stakes jobs—they all have the same goal: to help us look past our blind spots and focus on what really matters.
Now, it’s totally normal to feel a little skeptical about systems. Most people worry they’ll lose their freedom, or that creativity will get boxed in. But the best systems are almost invisible. They work quietly in the background, supporting your good decisions and catching the little errors that could cause big problems later on.
It really comes down to balance—finding that sweet spot between structure and spontaneity. If you clamp down too hard, intuition can’t breathe. But if you let everything run wild, chaos isn’t far behind. The goal isn’t to shut down your instincts, but to put up just enough guardrails so your natural strengths can shine, safely and reliably.
